description:
About the Team&Challenge We use AI and multi-source satellites (radar/optical) to map irrigated vs. non-irrigated lands, tackling water scarcity in Egypt. Our automated tool provides real-time data, overcoming cloud cover and reporting delays.

Required Resources & Data: Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2/Landsat, NASA GPM, & labeled datasets (IrrMap). 

Team HydroScan AI: We are CS & AI  engineers fusing satellite data with Deep Learning to map irrigation and solve water scarcity.
summary: HydroScan AI is a decision-support platform that helps arid-region farmers in Egypt see where fields are truly irrigated and decide what to plant next. It fuses Sentinel-1 radar and Sentinel-2 optical imagery with a Random Forest model to detect human-driven irrigation, validates it against NASA rainfall and soil-moisture data, then applies a transparent, rule-based agronomic engine to recommend crop rotations farmers can understand and trust.
details:
The problem. In Egypt, over 95% of fresh water comes from a single source, the Nile, and agriculture consumes most of it. Farmers on the desert fringe make costly planting and irrigation decisions with little data, while planners cannot easily tell which green fields are truly irrigated and which are simply greened by rain.

What HydroScan AI does. The user selects a farm or region on an interactive map. The platform (1) pulls satellite time series, (2) classifies where human-driven irrigation is happening, (3) checks that signal against NASA climate data, and (4) outputs a crop-rotation recommendation with the reasoning shown, not hidden.

How it works (architecture).

1.     Data layer: Google Earth Engine (GEE) delivers Sentinel-1 SAR (backscatter, works through cloud and at night) and Sentinel-2 optical bands/indices (vegetation and moisture signals) for the selected area, exported as a multi-band raster stack and time series.

2.     Irrigation detection: A Scikit-learn Random Forest classifier labels pixels as human-irrigated vs. not. We chose Random Forest deliberately: it trains fast on a small, hand-labelled dataset, handles mixed SAR and optical features well, gives feature importances, and made a working MVP possible within the hackathon.

3.     NASA validation layer: GPM rainfall and SMAP soil moisture confirm that green fields stay green without rain, so detected vegetation is human-irrigated rather than rain-fed.

4.     Rule-based Agronomic Engine: Crop rotation is not a black box. We designed a deterministic engine in which explicit thresholds (temperature windows from NASA POWER, moisture and season conditions) map to crop recommendations. Every recommendation can be traced to the exact rule that fired, so a farmer or an agronomist can audit, challenge and tune it.

5.     Interface: A Streamlit web app with Folium maps, with raster outputs aligned to the map using Rasterio.

Why this design wins in practice. Machine learning is used where patterns are hard to hand-code (reading irrigation from satellite signals). Rules are used where trust and accountability matter (telling a farmer what to plant). Explainability is a feature, not an afterthought.

Our team's role. We planned the system architecture, defined the labelling approach, designed the rule logic and set the environmental thresholds ourselves. We also diagnosed and fixed the geospatial alignment problems between Rasterio rasters and Folium map coordinates (CRS and bounds mismatches) that made overlays appear shifted.

Tools & languages: Python, Streamlit, Folium, Rasterio, Scikit-learn, Google Earth Engine API, Pandas/NumPy.

Limitations (honest scope). The model is an MVP trained on a limited set of labelled areas; it needs wider labelling and field validation before operational use. Our next steps: more regions and seasons, crop-type classification, and farmer feedback loops.
dataRefs: NASA SMAP L4 SPL4SMGP v8 (surface soil moisture)
NASA POWER Daily API (temperature T2M and rainfall PRECTOTCORR)
